details:
**Baha'u'llah**
The Persian founder of the Baha'i Faith (born Mirza Husayn-Ali; his title means "Glory of God"). While imprisoned in Tehran's Siyah-Chal ("Black Pit") dungeon in 1852, he had a vision of the "Maid of Heaven" announcing his mission. He was later exiled and spent over a decade imprisoned in Acre, and his shrine at nearby Bahji is the Qiblih that Baha'is face in daily prayer.

**Universal House of Justice**
The supreme elected governing body of the Baha'i Faith, seated at the Baha'i World Centre on Mount Carmel in Haifa, Israel. It was first elected in 1963, after the death of Shoghi Effendi, and it issues messages to Baha'is each Ridvan as well as statements such as "The Promise of World Peace."

**Book of Certitude (Kitab-i-Iqan)**
Baha'u'llah's main doctrinal work, setting out progressive revelation: God's messengers appear one after another, and the world's religions are stages of a single faith. A section on the "true seeker" describes the qualities of someone searching for God, such as detachment and avoiding "fellowship with evildoers." It is a separate book from the Kitab-i-Aqdas.

**Festival of Ridvan**
A twelve-day festival (April 21 to May 2, falling in the Baha'i months of Jalal and Jamal) marking the 1863 stay of Baha'u'llah in the Najibiyyih Garden on the banks of the Tigris near Baghdad, which he called Ridvan ("Paradise"). There he declared that he was "He whom God shall make manifest," the figure foretold by the Bab. The first, ninth, and twelfth days are holy days on which work is suspended.

**Shoghi Effendi**
Abdu'l-Baha's grandson, appointed the first and only Guardian of the faith, who led it from 1921 until his death in 1957. He translated key texts such as the Book of Certitude and the Epistle to the Son of the Wolf into English, wrote the history "God Passes By," and launched the Ten Year Crusade.

**Nineteen months of nineteen days**
The Baha'i calendar divides the year into 19 months of 19 days, plus four or five intercalary days called Ayyam-i-Ha, a time of gift-giving. The final month, 'Ala ("Loftiness"), is a 19-day sunrise-to-sunset fast that ends with the new year (Naw-Ruz). The number nineteen, sacred in the Babi and Baha'i faiths, recurs throughout.

**Hands of the Cause and the Ten Year Crusade**
The Hands of the Cause of God are eminent Baha'is appointed to spread and protect the faith. After Shoghi Effendi died in 1957, a group of them called the Custodians led the faith and completed his Ten Year (World) Crusade (1953–1963), a global teaching plan that ended with the first election of the Universal House of Justice. Their work was later continued by the Institution of the Counsellors.

**The Seven Valleys**
A mystical work by Baha'u'llah, written in answer to questions from Sufis, describing the soul's journey to God through seven stages, ending in the valley "of True Poverty and Absolute Nothingness." It is often paired with his "Four Valleys."

**Manifestations of God**
Prophets through whom God progressively reveals Himself, including Adam, Abraham, Moses, Zoroaster, Krishna, Buddha, Jesus, Muhammad, the Bab, and Baha'u'llah. This underlies the faith's core teaching of the "three onenesses": the oneness of God, of humanity, and of religion.

**The Bab**
Siyyid Ali-Muhammad (Mirza 'Ali-Muhammad) of Shiraz, whose title means "the Gate." In 1844 he founded Babism, which grew out of the Shaykhi school of Shia Islam, and organized his first eighteen disciples as the Letters of the Living. He was executed in 1850 after the first firing squad volley failed and he briefly vanished; Baha'is commemorate his Declaration on May 22–23, and both faiths have been persecuted in Shia-majority Iran.

**Kitab-i-Aqdas**
The "Most Holy Book," Baha'u'llah's book of laws, which Baha'is believe supersedes earlier revelations. Shoghi Effendi called it the "Charter of the future world civilization," and it is published with a Synopsis and Codification of its laws.

**Lotus Temple**
The Baha'i House of Worship in New Delhi, India, shaped like a lotus flower from 27 free-standing marble-clad "petals." Like all Baha'i Houses of Worship, including the one in Wilmette, Illinois, it is nine-sided and open to people of all religions.

**Epistle to the Son of the Wolf**
Baha'u'llah's last major work, addressed to a persecuting Muslim cleric whose father he called "the Wolf." It mourns the unjust execution of two Baha'i brothers in Isfahan, the Nahri brothers.

**Nine-pointed star and the Ringstone symbol**
The nine-pointed star is the most common symbol of the faith, since nine signifies completeness. The Ringstone symbol, designed by Abdu'l-Baha, shows three horizontal bars for the worlds of God, His Cause, and humanity, flanked by two stars (haykal) representing the Bab and Baha'u'llah.

**Abdu'l-Baha**
Baha'u'llah's eldest son and successor, the second leader of the faith. He wrote "The Secret of Divine Civilization" and the Tablet to The Hague, and his talks in France were published by Sara Louisa Blomfield as "Paris Talks."
